title: What makes a good prompt (and what makes a bad one)
description: Learn the core principles that separate prompts that get brilliant results from ones that get generic waffle. Includes before-and-after examples you can try right now.
content:
I want to start with something that surprises most people: the difference between a great AI result and a terrible one almost never comes down to the AI. It comes down to the prompt.

Think of it this way. If you walked up to a stranger and said 'Write me something about marketing', you would get a puzzled look. But if you said 'I run a small bakery in Manchester and I need three Instagram post ideas for Valentine's Day that sound warm and personal, not corporate' - now they can actually help you.

AI works the same way. It is not a mind reader. It is a brilliant assistant that needs clear instructions.

**The five elements of a good prompt**

Every effective prompt includes some combination of these five things:

1. **Role** - who you want the AI to be ('You are an experienced email copywriter')
2. **Task** - what you want it to do ('Write a follow-up email to a client who has gone quiet')
3. **Context** - background information ('The client is a small law firm, we last spoke three weeks ago about a website redesign')
4. **Format** - how you want the output ('Keep it under 100 words, friendly but professional tone')
5. **Constraints** - what to avoid ('Do not sound pushy or desperate, no exclamation marks')

You do not need all five every time, but the more you include, the better your results.

**Before and after: real examples**

Bad prompt: 'Write me a blog post about productivity.'

This will give you a generic 500-word article that could have been written about anyone, for anyone. It is technically correct and completely useless.

Good prompt: 'You are a business coach who works with small business owners in the UK. Write a 600-word blog post titled "5 productivity mistakes I see every week" in a conversational, first-person style. Use real-world examples like missed deadlines and overflowing inboxes. The reader is a busy founder who does not have time for theory - they want practical tips they can use today. Use UK English.'

The difference is night and day. Same AI, same tool, completely different output.

**The golden rule**

Here it is: **the more specific you are, the better the output**. Vague prompts get vague answers. Specific prompts get useful answers.

This does not mean your prompts need to be long. It means they need to be clear. 'Write a professional email declining a meeting request, keep it to two sentences, warm but firm' is only 18 words but it is very specific.

**Your first exercise**

Take something you would normally ask AI to do - writing an email, creating a social post, summarising notes - and before you hit send, ask yourself:

- Have I said who the audience is?
- Have I said what tone I want?
- Have I given any context about my situation?
- Have I said what format I want?

If you have not, add those details. Then compare the results. You will be genuinely surprised.

Once you see the difference, you will never go back to vague prompts again. And the best part? Every other technique in this library builds on this foundation. Get this right, and everything else becomes easier.
howToUse: Read the article and understand the five elements of a good prompt
Try the before-and-after examples with your preferred AI tool
Practice with your own real tasks using the exercise at the end

title: The role technique - why giving AI a character changes everything
description: Discover how assigning a role or persona to AI dramatically improves output quality. Learn when to use roles, which roles work best, and how to write effective role assignments.
content:
If I could only teach you one prompting technique, it would be this one. Giving AI a role before asking it to do anything is the single most effective way to improve your results.

Here is what I mean. Instead of saying 'Write me a product description', you say 'You are a senior e-commerce copywriter who specialises in converting browsers into buyers. Write me a product description for...'

That one extra sentence changes the entire output. But why?

**Why roles work so well**

When you assign a role, you are not just being creative - you are activating a specific set of knowledge and a specific way of thinking. An 'experienced HR manager' writes differently to a 'startup founder'. A 'sympathetic customer service agent' responds differently to a 'direct business consultant'.

The role acts as a filter for everything that follows. It tells the AI: of all the knowledge you have, focus on THIS expertise. Of all the ways you could write, write like THIS person would.

**How to write a good role assignment**

A strong role has three components:

1. **Experience level** - 'experienced', 'senior', 'expert', 'specialist'. This affects the depth and confidence of the output
2. **Specific expertise** - not just 'a marketer' but 'a B2B SaaS marketer who focuses on LinkedIn content'. The more specific, the more targeted the output
3. **Key qualities** - add personality traits that matter: 'who values clarity over jargon', 'who explains complex topics simply', 'who is warm but direct'

**Real examples that work**

- 'You are a CFO who explains financial concepts to non-finance team members in plain English'
- 'You are a recruitment consultant with 15 years of experience writing job descriptions that attract diverse candidates'
- 'You are a food photographer's assistant who writes Instagram captions that make people want to visit the restaurant'
- 'You are a patient, experienced primary school teacher explaining a concept to a curious 8-year-old'

Notice how each of these immediately sets expectations for tone, complexity, and approach.

**Common mistakes with roles**

The biggest mistake is being too vague. 'You are a writer' does almost nothing. 'You are a writer' activates generic writing knowledge. 'You are a conversion copywriter who writes landing pages for SaaS products' activates specific, useful knowledge.

Another mistake is assigning a role that contradicts your request. If you say 'You are an academic researcher' and then ask for a casual social media post, the AI will struggle with the mismatch.

**When not to use a role**

Roles are less useful for simple, factual tasks. If you are asking 'What is the capital of France?' you do not need a role. But for anything creative, strategic, or communication-based - which is most business use cases - a role makes a significant difference.

**Try it yourself**

Take any prompt you have used recently and add a role at the start. Run both versions and compare. I have done this hundreds of times and the role version wins every single time.

The role technique is so powerful that you will see it in almost every prompt in this library. Once you start using it, you will wonder how you ever prompted without it.
howToUse: Read the article and understand the three components of a good role assignment
Try the examples with your preferred AI tool and compare results with and without roles
Practice writing role assignments for your own common tasks

title: How to iterate - why your first prompt is just the start
description: Learn why treating AI as a conversation rather than a one-shot tool transforms your results. Master the art of follow-up prompts, refinement, and building on what the AI gives you.
content:
Here is a mindset shift that will change how you use AI: your first prompt is not the finish line. It is the starting line.

Most people type a prompt, get a result, and either accept it or give up. They are leaving 80% of the value on the table. The real magic happens in the follow-up.

**Think of it as a conversation, not a command**

When you brief a human colleague, you do not expect perfection on the first draft. You review their work, give feedback, and ask for revisions. AI works the same way - and it is actually better at taking feedback than most humans.

The key difference is that AI does not get offended, does not forget your feedback, and responds in seconds. So you can iterate much faster than you could with a person.

**The three types of follow-up prompts**

1. **Refining the output** - making what you got better
   - 'Make this more concise - cut it by 40%'
   - 'The tone is too formal, make it sound like I am talking to a friend'
   - 'Good structure, but add a real-world example to each section'

2. **Redirecting** - changing direction based on what you saw
   - 'Actually, focus more on the second point - that is the strongest one'
   - 'This is good but it is aimed at beginners. Rewrite it for people who already have some experience'
   - 'Can you take a completely different angle on this?'

3. **Expanding** - building on a strong result
   - 'Great. Now write three variations of the headline'
   - 'Turn point 3 into a full paragraph with more detail'
   - 'Write a follow-up email that references this one'

**My typical workflow**

When I am writing anything important, my process looks like this:

1. First prompt: get the rough structure and content (I call this the 'clay on the wheel')
2. Second prompt: refine the tone and fix anything that feels off
3. Third prompt: tighten the language, cut the waffle, strengthen the opening
4. Fourth prompt (sometimes): generate alternatives for key sections

Four prompts might sound like a lot, but each one takes about 10 seconds to write and the AI responds in seconds. The whole process takes 2-3 minutes and produces something dramatically better than the first draft.

**Follow-up prompts that always work**

Keep these in your back pocket:

- 'Make it shorter' (AI almost always overexplains)
- 'Make it more specific - use concrete examples instead of general statements'
- 'Remove the corporate jargon and write it in plain English'
- 'What would make this more persuasive?'
- 'Rewrite this but make it sound more like [a real person / a specific brand]'
- 'This is 7 out of 10 - what would make it a 9?'

That last one is my favourite. Asking the AI to improve its own work with a specific quality target often produces the best results of the entire conversation.

**The mistake to avoid**

Do not start a brand new conversation for each iteration. Keep refining within the same chat. The AI remembers everything you have discussed, so each follow-up builds on the context from before. Starting fresh means losing all that accumulated understanding.

**Your exercise**

Next time you use AI, commit to sending at least three follow-up prompts before accepting the result. Notice how much better the third version is compared to the first. That gap is what most people miss.
howToUse: Read the article and understand the three types of follow-up prompts
Try the workflow on a real task - first prompt, then refine, then tighten
Practice with the 'always work' follow-up prompts on your next AI interaction

title: Giving examples - the fastest way to get AI to match your style
description: Learn how providing examples (few-shot prompting) is the quickest way to get AI to write in your voice, match a specific format, or replicate a style. No technical knowledge needed.
content:
I am going to share the technique that made the biggest difference to my own AI results. It is deceptively simple: show the AI what you want by giving it examples.

This is called 'few-shot prompting' in technical circles, but forget that name. All you need to remember is: instead of describing what you want, show it.

**Why examples beat descriptions every time**

Imagine trying to explain your brand voice to a new copywriter. You could spend 20 minutes describing it - 'friendly but professional, a bit witty, never too formal, uses short sentences...' Or you could hand them three emails you have written and say 'Write like this.'

The second approach is faster, clearer, and produces better results. AI is exactly the same.

**How to use examples in your prompts**

The structure is simple:

'Here are some examples of [what I want]:

Example 1: [paste an example]
Example 2: [paste another example]

Now write [your request] in the same style.'

That is it. The AI will analyse the patterns in your examples - tone, sentence length, vocabulary, structure, formatting - and replicate them in new content.

**Real examples of this in action**

Matching your email style:
'Here are two emails I have written to clients that I was happy with:

[Email 1]
[Email 2]

Now write a follow-up email to a client who has not responded to our proposal in two weeks. Match the tone and style of my examples.'

Matching a social media format:
'Here are three LinkedIn posts that performed well for me:

[Post 1]
[Post 2]
[Post 3]

Write a new post about [topic] using the same structure, length, and tone.'

Matching a report format:
'Here is how I structure my weekly reports:

[Example report]

Using this exact format, write this week's report based on the following notes: [your notes]'

**How many examples do you need?**

One example is better than none. Two examples help the AI identify patterns. Three examples are usually enough for excellent results. More than five rarely adds much benefit.

The sweet spot for most tasks is two to three examples.

**What makes a good example?**

Your examples should be:
- **Representative** - typical of what you want, not outliers
- **High quality** - if you give the AI a badly written example, it will replicate the bad writing
- **Complete** - show the full piece, not just a snippet, so the AI can see the structure
- **Varied enough** - if all three examples are identical, the AI learns less than if they show slight variations

**The power move: negative examples**

You can also show the AI what you do NOT want:

'Here is an example of the style I want to avoid:
[Bad example]

And here is the style I want to match:
[Good example]

Write [your request] in the second style, not the first.'

This contrast helps the AI understand not just what to do, but what not to do.

**Your exercise**

Find three pieces of content you have written that you are proud of. Save them somewhere easy to access. Next time you ask AI to write something, paste them in as examples. Compare the result to what you get without examples.

Once you see the difference, you will start building a personal library of examples for different types of content. That library becomes your secret weapon.
howToUse: Read the article and understand how and why examples improve AI output
Try the technique with your own content - emails, posts, or reports you have written
Build a personal library of 'example' content for your most common AI tasks

title: Setting constraints - how limits actually improve output
description: Learn why telling AI what NOT to do is just as important as telling it what to do. Master the art of using word counts, formats, tone restrictions, and audience parameters to get better results.
content:
This is going to sound counterintuitive: giving AI more restrictions produces better output, not worse.

Think about it in human terms. If I ask you to 'write something', you are paralysed by choice. If I ask you to 'write a 50-word Instagram caption about our new product launch, aimed at millennials who care about sustainability, in a playful tone, without using the word eco-friendly' - you know exactly what to write.

Constraints are not limitations. They are clarity.

**The six types of useful constraints**

1. **Length constraints** - the most powerful and underused
   - 'Keep this under 100 words'
   - 'Write exactly 3 bullet points'
   - 'The email should be no longer than 5 sentences'
   
   AI naturally overexplains. Giving a word count forces it to be concise and prioritise what matters.

2. **Format constraints** - structure the output
   - 'Use bullet points, not paragraphs'
   - 'Structure this as: problem, solution, benefit'
   - 'Present this as a table with these columns...'
   - 'Write this as a numbered list of steps'

3. **Tone constraints** - control how it sounds
   - 'Conversational, like talking to a colleague over coffee'
   - 'Professional but warm - not corporate'
   - 'Direct and confident, no hedging or qualifiers'
   - 'Empathetic but not patronising'

4. **Audience constraints** - who is reading this
   - 'Written for someone who has never used this software before'
   - 'For a senior executive who has 30 seconds to scan this'
   - 'For a teenager who finds most business content boring'

5. **Content constraints** - what to include or exclude
   - 'Do not include an introduction - start with the first point directly'
   - 'No jargon - if a 12-year-old would not understand a word, do not use it'
   - 'Include specific numbers and examples, not vague generalisations'
   - 'Do not mention competitors by name'

6. **Style constraints** - specific writing rules
   - 'Use active voice throughout'
   - 'No sentences longer than 20 words'
   - 'Start each section with a question'
   - 'Use UK English spelling'

**The constraint I use most often**

'Make it shorter.'

Seriously. AI's default is to write too much. The first thing I do with almost any output is ask it to cut the length by 30-40%. The result is almost always better - tighter, punchier, and more useful.

**Stacking constraints for precision**

The real power comes from combining constraints. Watch how this builds:

Basic: 'Write a product description'
Better: 'Write a product description under 80 words'
Even better: 'Write a product description under 80 words for a premium audience'
Best: 'Write a product description under 80 words for a premium audience. Use short, confident sentences. No exclamation marks. Focus on how the product feels to use, not technical specifications. End with a single-sentence call to action.'

Each constraint adds focus. By the final version, the AI knows exactly what you want.

**The beginner's constraint starter pack**

If you remember nothing else from this article, add these three constraints to every prompt:

1. A word count or length limit
2. Who the audience is
3. One thing to avoid

Those three additions will improve 90% of AI outputs immediately.

**Your exercise**

Take any prompt you use regularly. Add three constraints from the list above. Run both versions and compare. Notice how the constrained version is more focused, more useful, and more like what you actually wanted.
howToUse: Read the article and understand the six types of useful constraints
Try adding the 'beginner's starter pack' (length, audience, avoidance) to your next prompt
Practice stacking constraints for increasingly precise results

title: Chain of thought - how to get AI to think step by step
description: Learn when and how to ask AI to show its working, break down complex problems, and think through tasks systematically. This technique turns AI from a quick answer machine into a genuine thinking partner.
content:
Most people use AI like a search engine - ask a question, get an answer. But for complex tasks, there is a technique that dramatically improves the quality of output: asking the AI to think step by step.

This is called 'chain of thought' prompting, and it works because it forces the AI to show its working, just like your maths teacher asked you to do at school.

**Why thinking step by step matters**

When you ask AI a complex question and expect an instant answer, it takes shortcuts. It jumps to conclusions. It misses nuances. But when you ask it to work through the problem step by step, it considers more angles, catches its own mistakes, and produces better reasoning.

The difference is especially noticeable for:
- Analysis and strategy questions
- Problem-solving and troubleshooting
- Decisions with multiple factors to weigh
- Planning and project breakdowns
- Anything where the 'right' answer depends on context

**How to trigger chain of thought**

The simplest version is just adding one phrase to your prompt:

'Think through this step by step before giving your final answer.'

That is genuinely all it takes. But you can be more specific:

- 'Break this problem down into steps. Consider each step separately before reaching a conclusion.'
- 'Before recommending a solution, first list the factors we need to consider, then evaluate each one, then give your recommendation.'
- 'Walk me through your reasoning. I want to understand how you reached your conclusion.'

**A real-world example**

Without chain of thought:
'Should I hire a full-time social media manager or outsource to an agency?'

The AI will give you a quick answer with some generic pros and cons. Useful, but shallow.

With chain of thought:
'I run a 15-person marketing consultancy. We currently spend about 5 hours per week on social media across LinkedIn and Instagram. We have a budget of roughly 30,000 pounds per year for this. Our content needs are mostly thought leadership posts and case studies. Think through this step by step - consider the cost comparison, quality considerations, management overhead, scalability, and risk factors. Then give me your recommendation with reasoning.'

The second version produces a genuinely useful analysis because it forces the AI to work through each factor systematically rather than jumping to a conclusion.

**When chain of thought is most valuable**

Use it when:
- The answer depends on multiple factors
- You need to weigh trade-offs
- The stakes are high and you want robust thinking
- You are trying to understand a complex topic
- You want to spot flaws in a plan

Do not bother when:
- The question has a simple, factual answer
- You just need a quick first draft
- Speed matters more than depth

**The advanced version: structured reasoning**

For really important decisions, give the AI a reasoning framework:

'Analyse this using the following structure:
1. First, identify the key question we are trying to answer
2. List all the relevant factors and evidence
3. Consider the strongest argument FOR this approach
4. Consider the strongest argument AGAINST this approach
5. Identify what we do not know that might change the answer
6. Give your recommendation with a confidence level (high, medium, low) and explain why'

This structured approach turns AI from a quick-answer machine into something much more like a genuine thinking partner.

**Your exercise**

Think of a decision you are currently facing in your business. Instead of asking AI 'What should I do?', ask it to think through the decision step by step. Provide context about your situation, constraints, and goals. Compare the depth of the response to what you would get from a simple question.

You will find the step-by-step version surfaces considerations you had not thought of. That is the real value.
howToUse: Read the article and understand when chain of thought prompting adds value
Try the simple trigger phrase on a real business decision
Practice the structured reasoning framework for important strategic questions

title: Context is king - how background information transforms results
description: Learn what context to provide, how much is enough, and how background information turns generic AI output into genuinely useful, personalised results for your specific situation.
content:
If there is one word that summarises everything about getting great results from AI, it is context. Context is the difference between generic advice you could find on any website and specific, actionable output tailored to your exact situation.

Here is the uncomfortable truth: when AI gives you a generic answer, it is usually because you gave it a generic prompt. The AI does not know about your business, your audience, your industry, or your constraints unless you tell it.

**What counts as context?**

Context is any background information that helps the AI understand your specific situation. There are five types:

1. **Who you are** - your role, business, industry, and experience level
   - 'I run a 10-person digital agency in Leeds that specialises in e-commerce'
   - 'I am a freelance graphic designer who works mainly with food and drink brands'

2. **Who the audience is** - who will read, see, or use the output
   - 'This is for small business owners who are not technical'
   - 'The audience is HR directors at companies with 500+ employees'

3. **What has already happened** - history and existing work
   - 'We tried Facebook ads last year but the cost per lead was too high'
   - 'Here is the email I sent last week that they have not replied to'

4. **What your constraints are** - budget, time, resources, rules
   - 'We have a budget of 2,000 pounds and need this done in two weeks'
   - 'It needs to comply with GDPR and our company cannot use customer names in marketing'

5. **What you have already tried** - so the AI does not suggest things you have already done
   - 'I have already considered SEO and decided against it for now'
   - 'We tried a similar approach in Q2 and it did not work because...'

**How context transforms output: a real example**

Without context:
'Give me ideas for growing my email list.'

You will get a generic listicle: create a lead magnet, add a pop-up form, run Facebook ads, guest post, etc. Technically correct. Practically useless because you have probably already read this advice 50 times.

With context:
'I run an independent physiotherapy practice in Bristol. I have 200 people on my email list, mostly existing patients. I want to grow to 1,000 in the next 6 months. My budget for this is about 200 pounds per month. I am already posting on Instagram (800 followers) and have a website that gets about 500 visits per month. I do not want to offer discounts as a lead magnet because it devalues the service. Most of my new patients come from GP referrals and word of mouth. Give me 5 specific ideas for growing my email list given this situation.'

The second prompt will produce ideas you have not thought of - specific to physiotherapy, specific to your budget, specific to your existing channels. That is the power of context.

**How much context is too much?**

I get asked this a lot and the honest answer is: it is very hard to give too much context. AI is excellent at filtering what is relevant. I have never seen a prompt fail because there was too much background information.

That said, you do not need to write an essay. A few sentences covering the five types above is usually enough. Think of it as a brief you would give a consultant who is helping you for the first time.

**The context checklist**

Before you send any important prompt, quickly scan this list:

- Have I said what my business does? Yes/No
- Have I said who the audience is? Yes/No
- Have I mentioned any relevant constraints? Yes/No
- Have I shared any relevant history? Yes/No
- Have I said what I have already tried? Yes/No

You do not need all five every time. But for important tasks, the more boxes you tick, the better your results.

**Your exercise**

Pick a task you often ask AI to help with. Write the prompt you normally use. Then add 3-5 sentences of context using the types above. Compare the outputs. The contextualised version will feel like it was written specifically for you - because it was.
howToUse: Read the article and understand the five types of context
Use the context checklist before your next important prompt
Practice adding context to prompts you already use and compare the difference

title: Advanced technique: meta-prompting - using AI to write your prompts for you
description: Learn the advanced technique of asking AI to help you write better prompts. This is where prompting goes from manual skill to multiplied capability - and a taste of what the full course covers.
content:
Here is something that might bend your brain a little: you can use AI to write better prompts for AI.

This is called meta-prompting, and it is genuinely one of the most powerful techniques I have come across. Once you understand it, you will never struggle to write a prompt again.

**The basic idea**

Instead of trying to write the perfect prompt yourself, you describe what you want to achieve and ask the AI to write the prompt for you. Then you use that generated prompt (tweaking it if needed) to get your actual output.

It sounds like an extra step, but it consistently produces better results than most people can write on their own - because AI knows what makes a good prompt.

**How to do it: the simple version**

'I want to [describe your goal]. Write me a detailed prompt that I could paste into ChatGPT to get the best possible result. Include a role, specific instructions, constraints, and output format.'

That is it. The AI will generate a prompt that is usually more detailed, better structured, and more effective than what you would have written.

**A real example**

Your goal: 'I need to write a case study about a project we did for a client'

Meta-prompt: 'I want to write a compelling case study about a project my agency completed for a client. Write me a detailed prompt I can use in ChatGPT to generate this case study. The prompt should include a role, ask me the right questions about the project, specify the format and structure, and include constraints about tone and length.'

The AI generates something like: 'You are a B2B content strategist who specialises in writing case studies that drive sales enquiries. Before writing, ask me about: the client's industry, the problem they faced, what we did, the results (with specific numbers), and a client quote. Write the case study in this structure: headline, client overview, the challenge, our approach, the results, client testimonial. Keep it under 600 words. Use a professional but conversational tone. Focus on outcomes rather than process. Include specific numbers wherever possible.'

That generated prompt is better than what most people would write from scratch. And it took 10 seconds.

**The advanced version: the prompt refiner**

You can also use meta-prompting to improve prompts you have already written:

'Here is a prompt I have been using: [paste your prompt]. How would you improve this to get better results? What am I missing? What could be more specific?'

The AI will analyse your prompt and suggest improvements you had not considered. This is like having a prompting coach available at all times.

**The ultra-advanced version: the prompt generator**

For complex, recurring tasks, you can create a 'prompt generator' - a meta-prompt that generates customised prompts based on a few inputs:

'I want you to be a prompt generator for writing marketing emails. When I give you a brief (audience, goal, product), create a complete, detailed prompt I can use to generate the email. Include role, context, instructions, constraints, and output format. Make the prompt specific enough to get a near-final draft on the first try.'

Now every time you need a marketing email, you just give the brief and get a tailored prompt. It is like building your own custom tool.

**Why this matters beyond just prompting**

Meta-prompting is important because it represents a shift in how we think about AI. You are not just using a tool - you are using a tool to build better tools. Each meta-prompt you create becomes a reusable asset. Over time, you build a library of refined prompts for every task you do regularly.

This is the difference between someone who uses AI occasionally and someone who has AI working as a genuine force multiplier in their business.

**What comes next**

This article has given you a taste of meta-prompting, but there is much more to explore. In the full Smash Your AI course, we go deep into advanced techniques - building custom prompt libraries, creating AI workflows that chain multiple prompts together, and designing systems where AI handles entire processes with minimal input.

If the fundamentals in this library have improved your results, the advanced techniques will transform how you work entirely.

**Your exercise**

Right now, think of a task you do frequently. Describe that task to AI and ask it to write you the perfect prompt for it. Use the generated prompt and compare the result to what you normally get. Then refine the generated prompt and save it for next time.

You have just started building your personal prompt library. That is where the real leverage begins.
howToUse: Read the article and understand the three levels of meta-prompting
Try the simple version on a real task - ask AI to write you a prompt, then use it
Practice the prompt refiner technique on prompts you already use regularly
